import { Canvas, Markdown, Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';
import * as CopyFromFieldStories from './copy-from-field.story';
import * as CopyFromMenuStories from './copy-from-menu.story';
import * as CopyToClipboardStories from './copy-to-clipboard.story';
import CopyFromFieldSource from './copy-from-field.tsx?raw';

import CopyFromMenuSource from './copy-from-menu.tsx?raw';

<Meta title="Design System/Patterns/Copy to Clipboard" tags={ [ 'manifest' ] } />

# Copy to Clipboard

Choose feedback that remains visible after the action runs. A control that stays on the page can confirm the copy itself. When a menu closes, a snackbar can keep the confirmation visible.

## Standalone button

Put the confirmation on the button so it stays with the control that produced the result. Use `variant="minimal"`, `tone="neutral"`, and `size="compact"`: a copy action is rarely the primary button on the page. Don't use a snackbar here: the button is still visible. Don't use a tooltip: touch users and many keyboard users never see it.

<Canvas
	of={ CopyToClipboardStories.CopyExample }
	source={ { code: CopyToClipboardSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

The visible label and the accessible name stay "Copy". A check icon shows success, and an error icon shows failure, so the control is not renamed while it has focus. Copy with `useCopyToClipboard` from `@wordpress/compose`, and use its `onError` callback when the write fails. Call `speak()` with "Copied to clipboard", or "Couldn't copy to clipboard." if copying fails, to announce the outcome politely. Focus stays on the button.

For an icon-only control, use `IconButton` with the same variant, tone, and size, and keep `label="Copy"`. That label is the accessible name and the tooltip. Swap the icon for a check on success or an error icon on failure, and announce the result with `speak()`. The success and error messages belong in that announcement rather than only in the tooltip.

Copying is a one-time action. `aria-pressed` describes a toggle that stays on or off, so this button does not use it.

Restart the two-second feedback timeout after each copy result, including repeated successes or failures, so the icon remains visible for the full two seconds after the latest attempt completes.

## Text field

When the value is in a text field, put the copy action in the field's suffix so it stays with the value. Don't use a snackbar here: the button is still visible.

<Canvas
	of={ CopyFromFieldStories.CopyFromField }
	source={ { code: CopyFromFieldSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

Copy the field's current value, so an edit is what gets copied. Use `readOnly: true` to disallow editing the field. A read-only input with a copy suffix might indicate that the design needs inline text and a copy button instead of an input. Use `IconButton` and keep `label="Copy"`. That label is the accessible name and the tooltip. A check icon shows success, and an error icon shows failure. Call `speak()` with "Copied to clipboard", or "Couldn't copy to clipboard." if copying fails.

## Copying from a menu

When a copy action appears inside a menu, the menu typically closes immediately after the action is activated. A snackbar can provide visual confirmation after the menu item disappears. Use the screen's existing snackbar region where available.

Consider the placement and timing concerns tracked in [Snackbar Accessibility Issues (#16549)](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/16549). A message far from the trigger can fall outside a person's magnified view, and an automatically dismissed message can disappear before they read or reach it. A polite announcement doesn't remove these concerns.

<Canvas
	of={ CopyFromMenuStories.CopyFromMenu }
	source={ { code: CopyFromMenuSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

This example uses `useCopyToClipboard` for the write and `SnackbarList` for the message. The list animates the snackbar in and out, and `Snackbar` announces "Link copied to clipboard", or "Couldn't copy link to clipboard." if copying fails, through its own polite live region. That region stays on the page after the menu closes, so the example does not add a second one. The item label stays "Copy link".

The local `SnackbarList` and its positioning styles keep this preview self-contained. In a WordPress screen, use `core/notices` to create notices with `type: 'snackbar'` for the screen's existing snackbar region instead of adding a second list.

## Guidance

<Markdown>{ `
| Context | Recommended feedback | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standalone copy button | Temporary check or error icon; the label stays "Copy" | The control remains visible. The name stays the action, and the icon shows success or failure. |
| Text field suffix | Temporary check or error icon on the suffix button; the accessible name stays "Copy" | The button remains visible beside the value. Copy the field's current value. |
| Copy action in a menu | The screen's existing snackbar region | The confirmation remains visible after the menu closes; assess its placement and timing. |
` }</Markdown>

- **Keep standalone feedback on the button.** A snackbar isn't needed when the button can show the result.
- **Keep field feedback on the suffix button.** The button stays visible beside the value, so it shows the result. Copy the field's current value.
- **Keep menu feedback visible after closing.** Use the screen's existing snackbar region and assess its placement and timing.
- **Always announce the outcome accessibly.** Visual feedback alone isn't sufficient.
- **Avoid redundant feedback.** Don't show both inline confirmation and a snackbar for the same action unless there's a compelling reason.

design-system-patterns-destructive-actio.content:
import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';

<Meta title="Design System/Patterns/Destructive Actions" tags={ [ 'manifest' ] } />

# Destructive Actions

Destructive actions are operations that remove, delete, or permanently alter content or data. The appropriate pattern to use depends on the reversibility and immediacy of the action's result.

## Decision Tree

When implementing a destructive action, follow this decision tree:

1. **Does the action have an immediate visible result on the frontend?**
   - If **no** → [No confirmation needed](#no-confirmation-needed)
   - If **yes** → Continue to question 2

2. **Can the action be easily undone?**
   - If **yes** → [Use confirmDialog](#use-confirmdialog)
   - If **no** → [Use Modal with destructive button](#use-modal-with-destructive-button)

## No Confirmation Needed

Destructive actions that have no immediate visible result on the frontend (e.g., deleting a block) do not require any destructive styling or confirmation.

### When to Use

- The action doesn't produce an immediate visible change on the frontend
- The action can be reversed through standard undo functionality
- The user expects the action to be reversible

### Implementation

- Use standard trigger styling, avoiding destructive (red) styling
- No confirmation dialog required
- Ensure undo functionality is available

**Example**: Deleting a block in the editor. The block is removed but the change can be immediately undone using the undo command.

## Use ConfirmDialog

Destructive actions that have an immediate visible result but can be easily undone (e.g., moving to trash) require a confirmation using the `ConfirmDialog` component. A snackbar with undo affordance should be displayed after the action completes.

### When to Use

- The action produces an immediate visible change
- The action can be reversed through a clear, accessible mechanism (e.g., trash/restore)
- The user should be aware of the change before it happens

### Implementation

- Use `__experimentalConfirmDialog` from `@wordpress/components`
- The dialog can be dismissed (ESC key, click outside, cancel button)
- Standard button styling for the trigger (no destructive styling)
- The confirmation button uses primary variant (not destructive)
- After the action completes, display a Snackbar with an undo action

### Component Details

`ConfirmDialog` is built on top of `Modal` and provides:
- Automatic focus management
- Keyboard navigation (Enter to confirm, ESC to cancel)
- Accessible dialog structure
- Standard button layout (Cancel + Confirm)

**Example**: Moving a post to trash. The post status changes immediately, but it can be restored from the trash.

## Use Modal with Destructive Button

Destructive actions that cannot be undone require a confirmation, but the primary action button should be `destructive`. Use `Modal` without a close button. A snackbar should confirm the action completes.

### When to Use

- The action produces an immediate, permanent change
- The action cannot be reversed or undone
- The consequences are significant and irreversible

### Implementation

- Use `Modal` component (not `ConfirmDialog`)
- Set `isDismissible={ false }` to prevent closing via the header button
- Set `shouldCloseOnEsc={ false }` to prevent closing via ESC key
- Set `shouldCloseOnClickOutside={ false }` to prevent closing via overlay click
- Primary action button must have `isDestructive={ true }` prop
- Cancel button should use `variant="tertiary"`
- User must explicitly choose Cancel or Delete (no accidental dismissal)
- After the action completes, display a Snackbar to confirm the action

### Component Details

The `Modal` configuration ensures:
- User cannot accidentally dismiss the dialog
- Destructive styling on the primary button clearly indicates danger
- User must make a deliberate choice to proceed or cancel
- Accessibility is maintained through proper ARIA attributes and focus management

### Accessibility Considerations

- The modal title should clearly describe the action
- Use descriptive button labels (e.g., "Delete permanently" not just "Delete")
- Ensure focus is properly managed when the modal opens

**Example**: Permanently deleting a post. The post is removed completely and cannot be restored.

## Additional Confirmation Patterns

For highly destructive or complex actions, an additional confirmation step may be warranted. Include an initially unchecked checkbox that the user must check before the destructive button becomes enabled. The checkbox label should explicitly state what the user is acknowledging (e.g., "I understand this action cannot be undone").

import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';

<Meta title="Design System/Patterns/Error Messages" tags={ [ 'manifest' ] } />

# Error Messages

An error message can be the only conversation a user has with the software when something breaks. A good one turns a dead end into a next step or an action item. These guidelines describe how to write error messages that explain what happened, why, and what the user can do about it.

See also: [Copy guide](docs/contributors/documentation/copy-guide.md).

## Anatomy of a good error message

A strong message answers three questions in order:

1. **What happened?** The outcome, stated plainly.
2. **Why?** The specific cause.
3. **What now?** One or more next steps to try.

> _\{Browser\} can't read \{format\} photos, so we couldn't convert this one. \{Supported option\} usually can, or \{fallback\} instead._

Keep it to a sentence or two. If a message needs a paragraph, the underlying flow probably needs rethinking more than the copy does.

## Principles

### Explain the _why_

Don't report only that something failed. Explain the reason, because the reason is usually what points to the fix.

If the cause genuinely isn't known, don't invent a plausible-sounding one. Say that something went wrong and still offer a next step, but a guessed reason that turns out wrong sends the user down the wrong path.

### Write it like you'd describe it to a friend

Use plain, natural language. Skip error codes, internal component names, and jargon. If you wouldn't say it out loud to a colleague looking over your shoulder, don't put it in the message. A little warmth (and even a little fun) is welcome: an error is a frustrating moment, and the tone can soften it.

### Don't blame the user

Keep the tone nonjudgmental and describe the situation, not a fault. Avoid words that pin the problem on the reader, such as _invalid_, _illegal_, _incorrect_, or phrasing it like "you failed to" or "you didn't." Say what needs to happen next instead: "Enter a date in the future," not "You entered an invalid date."

### Be specific

Vague subjects ("this browser", "the server", "something") force the user to guess. Name the thing that didn't work: the specific browser, platform, file type, or field. Specificity also makes the message searchable and easier for the user to reason about.

### Offer a way forward

Every error should leave the user with at least one thing to try next: a supported alternative, a format that will work, a setting to change. When you name a constraint, name the escape from it also.

### Fail gracefully

When something goes wrong, minimize harm or exposure. Preserve the user's work, avoid destructive side effects, and never leak sensitive or internal details in the message.

### Make errors easy to act on

A message the user can't read or copy isn't actionable:

-   **Persist it.** Errors that require a decision should not auto-dismiss. Give the user time to read, understand, and act.
-   **Place it near the problem.** If possible, place the message where the failure happened.
-   **Let people copy it.** Optionally offer a copy-to-clipboard affordance so users can paste messages into search, documentation, or an AI assistant.

See [Notice with disclosed details](?path=/docs/design-system-components-notice-disclosure--docs) for an example using native details to reveal supplementary text, with a text button to copy the message and details.

## Displaying error messages

1.  **Does the user have to make a decision?** If not, use a [`Snackbar`](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/components-snackbar--docs). It clears itself after after a short delay.
2.  If yes, **Can you show where the failure happened?** Then do that: render a [`Notice`](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/components-notice--docs) with `status="error"` in the block, panel, or row that failed, rather than at the top of the screen. For invalid fields on save or submit, follow the [Save & Submit](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-patterns-save-submit--docs) pattern, which scrolls to the first field and shows the message there.
3.  **Does it affect the whole screen?** Use a `Notice` at the top of the screen, below any toolbars. It persists until dismissed or resolved.
4.  **Must it be resolved before the user can continue?** Use a `Modal`, not a `Notice`. See the [`Notice` guidelines](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/components-notice--docs).

Note: if a Snackbar's position is right but its timer isn't, set `explicitDismiss` to keep it on screen until the user closes it.

import { Canvas, Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';
import * as SaveSubmitStories from './save-and-submit.story';

<Meta title="Design System/Patterns/Save & Submit" tags={ [ 'manifest' ] } />

# Save & Submit

Guidelines for saving settings and submitting forms.

Editing a document, such as a post and its blocks, follows a different model: changes apply to the content straight away and are saved together with the document. These guidelines don’t cover that model.

## Choose one save model per surface

Before designing anywhere people change settings, such as a screen, a panel, or a modal, make a deliberate choice: does the surface **collect changes behind an explicit “Save changes” button**, or does it **save automatically** as the user makes changes?

Pick one for the entire surface. **Do not mix the two.** A page where some fields save instantly while others wait for a button leaves the user unable to tell what has actually been saved and what is still pending. This is the core reason mixed saving feels unreliable. Mixing also undermines the unsaved-changes prompt: a warning that only covers some of the fields gives false reassurance about the rest.

A surface is a region whose save state is communicated by a single control: either one Save button, or the absence of any. Usually that is the whole screen, panel, or modal. A screen can occasionally be split into separate surfaces, for example a card of instantly applied switches beside a form with its own Save button, but only when the regions are visually distinct and each makes its model obvious. Treat this as the exception, not a way to mix models within one form.

-   **Manual save** is the usual choice in WordPress. It is the right one when changes are interdependent and should apply together, when saving has side effects that are better batched into a single action, or when the environment submits a whole form at once (for example, classic WordPress admin screens, or third-party pages that post to PHP).
-   **Autosave** suits surfaces whose fields can be validated and persisted independently and asynchronously, such as a list of preferences that each take effect on their own (for example, the block editor’s Preferences modal). Changes save as they’re made, so there is no Save button, and no unsaved-changes prompt unless an edit fails to save.

Choose the model that fits how the surface’s data is saved, and commit to it across every field on the surface.

## Manual save model

Edits are held locally and applied together when the user clicks a single primary **Save changes** button.

<Canvas of={ SaveSubmitStories.SaveFormLayoutCard } />

### Saving

-   While saving, the [`Button`](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-components-button--docs) switches to its `loading` state and can’t be clicked again.
-   A [Snackbar](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/components-snackbar--docs) confirms a successful save.

### No unsaved changes

When all changes are saved, the Save button is disabled. A disabled Save on a form with no changes is a familiar convention and needs no explanation. If a disabled state does need explaining, use inline text, not a [`Tooltip`](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-components-tooltip--docs): tooltips aren't available to screen readers or on touch devices.

### Unsaved changes on exit

If the user navigates away with unsaved edits, prompt them to confirm before leaving so their changes aren’t lost. This guard belongs to the manual save model. An autosave surface only needs it while a text field holds an edit that failed to save (see [Autosave model](#autosave-model)).

-   **Only ask when something would be lost.** Prompt only while there are unsaved edits. Once the user saves, or changes a field back to its saved value, navigation is free again.
-   **Inside the app, use an [`AlertDialog`](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-components-alertdialog--docs).** Hold the navigation (switching between adjacent pages, following a breadcrumb or opening a record) and ask “Discard unsaved changes?” with the `irreversible` intent, because leaving discards the edits and can’t be undone. Offer two choices: “Keep editing”, which cancels the navigation and is the safe default, and “Discard changes”, which continues. Don’t add a “Save and leave” option: a save can fail validation, and the dialog is the wrong place to show that.
-   **When leaving the app, rely on the browser.** Reloading, closing the tab or following an external link can only be guarded with the `beforeunload` event, which shows the browser’s own warning. Its wording can’t be customized, so don’t try to imitate it.
-   **Dialogs and drawers that hold a draft close only through their actions.** Give them a footer with Cancel and Save, and omit the close icon and closing by clicking outside, so the user always makes an explicit choice. Cancel discards the draft without asking again, because choosing it is the decision. If the user presses Escape with unsaved edits, ask with the same dialog before closing.

Edit the title below, then click “Back”:

<Canvas of={ SaveSubmitStories.UnsavedChangesOnExit } />

### Invalid fields, partial saves, and failed saves

Keep the Save button enabled when fields are invalid, so that clicking it can explain what needs fixing. When it is clicked:

-   Show each error message right below its field.
-   Move focus to the first invalid field, scrolling it into view.
-   Don’t send the save until the errors are fixed.

A form’s native validation does this for you: wrap the fields in a `<form>` and make Save a `type="submit"` button, so pressing Enter in a field submits too. Controls built on `ControlWithError` show their message and move focus. They also show a message as soon as focus leaves an invalid field, so place Save above the fields, for example in the card or page header, where a new message can’t push it away mid-click. Clear the site title below, then click “Save changes”:

<Canvas of={ SaveSubmitStories.InvalidFields } />

If the save goes through but only some changes succeed, show a single [`Notice`](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-components-notice--docs) at the top of the form that says what saved and what still needs attention. List every area that needs attention in that one `Notice`, and never show a success message and an error message together.

If the save fails entirely, keep the user’s edits so they can retry, and show the reason in the `Notice`.

## Autosave model

Each change is persisted as it is made. There is no Save button, and no unsaved-changes guard while every change has saved.

<Canvas of={ SaveSubmitStories.AutosaveFeatureList } />

-   **Switches, selects, and radios** save immediately on change.
-   **Text and number fields** save on blur, or debounced after the user stops typing, never on every keystroke.
-   **Per-field errors.** If a save fails, show the error at the field and let the user retry. A failure on one field must not block editing the others.
    -   For a switch, select, or radio, return the control to its saved value, so it never shows a state that wasn’t saved.
    -   For a text or number field, keep what the user entered so it isn’t lost, and mark the field as not saved until a retry succeeds.
    -   After “Try again”, move focus to the field it retried. The retry removes its notice, and focus would otherwise fall back to the page.
-   **No global Save button.** It implies pending state that this model doesn’t have.
-   **No unsaved-changes prompt while everything has saved.** The exception is a text or number field that failed to save: the field holds the user’s only copy of the edit. If the user navigates away, keep that edit so they can retry when they come back, or ask “Discard unsaved changes?” before throwing it away.

In this example, saving “Show related posts” always fails. Flip it to see the switch return to its saved value, with an error `Notice` below it:

<Canvas of={ SaveSubmitStories.AutosaveFailure } />

Because autosave depends on fields saving independently, it isn’t suitable when several fields must be validated or applied together. Those cases call for the manual save model.

## Switches

A switch implies immediate effect, like a light switch, so **only use a switch where flipping it takes effect immediately**:

- **On an autosave surface, use a switch.** Flipping it saves the change. Use [`SwitchControl`](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-components-form-switchcontrol--docs) for turning features on and off.
- **In an editor, such as the block settings sidebar, use a switch.** The change applies to the content straight away, even though it is saved with the document later.
- **On a manual-save surface, don’t use a switch.** Nothing happens until the Save button is clicked, so a switch would either save on its own, mixing the two models, or wait for the button and contradict what it implies. Use [`CheckboxControl`](https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-components-form-checkboxcontrol--docs) for the same on and off choices, so they are applied together with the rest of the form.

Keep switch labels short. Name the setting, such as “Lazy loading”, or lead with a verb, such as “Allow comments”. Use the switch’s `description` or the card title to provide more context.

<Meta title="Design System/Patterns/Settings Page" tags={ [ 'manifest' ] } />

# Settings Page

Templates for settings screens, composed from the admin-ui `Page`, `@wordpress/ui` components, `@wordpress/theme` tokens and DataViews. Start from the template closest to your settings, then replace the fields.

These templates are starting points, not requirements. Not every settings page needs to match one exactly: adapt the structure to what your settings need, and combine or depart from the templates where that serves people better.

Several of the `@wordpress/ui` components they use, including `Button`, `Dialog`, `Drawer` and `AlertDialog`, are still marked “Use with caution”, so their APIs may change. Treat the templates as the direction settings pages are heading, not as a recommendation to migrate existing screens yet.

## Building blocks

Every template uses the same parts:

-   **`Page`** from `@wordpress/admin-ui` provides the header: a title or breadcrumbs, optional section navigation, and the actions area where Save lives.
-   **`Card`** from `@wordpress/ui` groups related settings. Give each card a short title, and a description when the title alone doesn't say what the settings affect. The Structure section below covers when to use one. Cap form cards at `--wpds-dimension-surface-width-xl` so fields stay a readable length, and give tables of records `--wpds-dimension-surface-width-2xl` so their columns fit.
-   **`DataForm`** from `@wordpress/dataviews` renders the fields, so labels, descriptions, validation and spacing stay consistent.
-   **`DataViews`** from `@wordpress/dataviews` lists records people can add and edit.
-   **`Dialog`**, **`Drawer`** and **`AlertDialog`** from `@wordpress/ui` hold record editors and confirmations.
-   **Snackbars** confirm saves that have no other visible effect. `SnackbarList` comes from `@wordpress/components`, since `@wordpress/ui` doesn't offer an equivalent yet.

Each example's code shows its template. The helpers it imports, such as the manual-save draft, the sample fields and the in-canvas router, live alongside it in `storybook/stories/design-system/patterns/settings-page/`.

## Structure

Plan a settings page like a document's outline before choosing how it looks. The headings decide how assistive technology reads the page and lets people jump through it, and the same kind of content should get the same treatment wherever it appears.

-   **Put each group of related fields in a card.** A card bounds a group and separates it from the groups around it. Keep the card even when a page has a single group, so every settings page reads the same way.
-   **Title each card after its group of fields.** The page title is the `h1`, and on a page without sections the card titles are `h2`s.
-   **Add sections when cards form larger groups.** A section heading sits on the canvas above its cards, as an `h2` with an optional description, and the cards inside it take `h3` titles. Use `Text` with `variant="heading-lg"` for the section heading. Each section gets its own heading, and a page with only a few cards needs none.
-   **Don't skip heading levels**, and don't choose a level for its size. The level follows the structure, so a card title looks the same whether it's an `h2` or an `h3`.

## Saving

These templates use the manual save model from [Save & Submit](?path=/docs/design-system-patterns-save-submit--docs): edits are held in a draft until the user clicks “Save changes”. Manual save is the usual choice for settings, because their fields often depend on each other and should apply together. Autosave suits a page of independent preferences that each take effect on their own, such as the block editor’s Preferences modal. Choose one model for the whole page and don't mix the two: if you choose autosave, remove the Save button. [Choose one save model per surface](?path=/docs/design-system-patterns-save-submit--docs#choose-one-save-model-per-surface) explains how to decide.

-   **One “Save changes” button per page**, in the `Page` header actions. It covers every field on that page and nothing else.
-   **Disabled only when there is nothing to save**, and busy while saving. Don't explain the disabled state with a tooltip: tooltips aren't available to screen readers or on touch devices.
-   **Invalid fields don't disable Save.** The fields sit in a `<form>`, and Save submits it: invalid fields show their errors below them and the first one takes focus, and nothing is saved until they're fixed. The record editors work the same way.
-   **Edits made while saving stay unsaved.** People can keep typing while a save is in progress. Once it finishes, anything they changed in the meantime is still an unsaved change, and a record editor stays open to hold it.
-   **Checkboxes, not switches, for on/off settings.** A switch implies the change takes effect immediately, which isn't true until Save is clicked. Switches belong on autosave surfaces.
-   **A snackbar confirms the save.** Errors belong next to the field, or in a `Notice` at the top of the form when a save fails or only partly succeeds.
-   **Pages that only list records have no page-level Save.** Each record editor saves on its own, and the header holds the action that adds a record.
-   **Leaving with unsaved edits asks first.** Switching pages, following a breadcrumb or closing a record editor with Escape asks “Discard unsaved changes?”, and reloading or closing the tab shows the browser’s own warning. Navigating while a save is in progress waits for it to finish, then asks only if something changed after clicking Save. Try it in any template by changing a field, then navigating away. See [Unsaved changes on exit](?path=/docs/design-system-patterns-save-submit--docs#unsaved-changes-on-exit).

### When a save fails

Keep the draft, so nothing the user entered is lost, and explain the failure in a `Notice` at the top of the form with a “Try again” action. Retrying submits the form again, so validation runs first. A retry that goes through removes the notice, and the focused button with it, so move focus to “Save changes” first. In this example the first save fails: change a field, click “Save changes”, then try again.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.FailedSave }
	source={ { code: FailedSaveSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

## Focus after navigation

Moving between adjacent pages and subpages replaces the page, including the link that was just used. Without help, keyboard focus falls back to the start of the document and screen readers don't announce the new page.

The templates' in-canvas router handles this: when a navigation removes the focused element, focus moves to the new page's `Page` region, and screen readers announce it by name. Try it by following a breadcrumb with the keyboard. `@wordpress/boot` currently updates and announces the route title, and will move focus the same way once [#86701](https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/86701) lands. Until then, or if your app routes without `@wordpress/boot`, move focus to the `Page` region yourself after each navigation that loses focus.

The region takes its name from `title`, so give it an `ariaLabel` whenever the title doesn't identify the page: on a subpage whose breadcrumbs replace the title, name it after the page, such as “Card payments”. On adjacent pages that share a title, name each one after its page, such as “Payments settings”.

## Simple settings page

A single page with a few groups of settings. Use it when everything fits on one screen.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.Simple }
	source={ { code: SimpleSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

## Settings page with sections

A longer page whose cards fall into larger groups, here "Accepting payments" and "Payouts". Each section has an `h2` heading on the canvas, and its cards take `h3` titles. Use it when one page holds several distinct areas, but they are too closely related, or too small, to split into adjacent pages.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.Sections }
	source={ { code: SectionsSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

## Adjacent pages

Peer sections of one settings area, such as General, Payments and Emails, switched with the `Page` `navigation`. Use it when the sections are independent and each one is substantial enough to deserve a page.

-   Keep the page title the same across adjacent pages; the navigation shows which page is current, so the title doesn't need to name it.
-   Each page has its own draft and Save. Saving one page doesn't save another.
-   Pass a router link through `components.link`, so switching pages doesn't reload the screen.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.AdjacentPages }
	source={ { code: AdjacentPagesSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

## Subpages

A subpage holds detail that would crowd the main page, such as the credentials for each payment gateway. Open it from the page body with a full-width row at the bottom of the card: a `Link` with `variant="unstyled"`, styled as a row, with a trailing chevron to signal that it navigates. A status badge in the row tells people what they will find there.

When a card leads to several subpages, put the rows in a list:

-   **Use a `ul`, named by the card title.** Render the title as a heading, and point the list's `aria-labelledby` at it, so screen readers announce “Payment gateways, list, 3 items”.
-   **Keep `role="list"` on the unstyled list.** Safari drops list semantics when the bullets are removed.
-   **Name each link after its destination.** The row label matches the subpage's heading, so the link's name is just “Card payments”. Show the status in a `Badge` and connect it with `aria-describedby`, so screen readers announce it as a description rather than as part of the name.

On the subpage, breadcrumbs replace the title and lead back to the parent page. Repeat the row's status next to the breadcrumbs with the `Page` `badges` prop, and update it from the saved settings, not the draft, so it changes when people click Save.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.Subpages }
	source={ { code: SubpagesSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

## Adjacent pages and subpages

When a subpage belongs to one of several adjacent pages, its trail passes through that page, for example "Settings / Payments / Card payments". "Payments" leads back to the page the subpage was opened from, with its navigation item current, and "Settings" leads to the first adjacent page. The subpage drops the section navigation.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.AdjacentPagesAndSubpages }
	source={ { code: AdjacentPagesAndSubpagesSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

## Records

Some settings are lists of records, such as API keys, webhooks or redirects. These examples use API keys. Show them in a `DataViews` table, and choose how each record opens by the size of its editor.

<Markdown>{ `
| Editor | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| Subpage | The editor is long, has its own sections, or people need to link to a record. |
| Dialog | The editor is short and people should stay focused on one record. |
| Drawer | The editor is medium-sized, people benefit from seeing the table, or the record has secondary actions. |
` }</Markdown>

### Records that open a subpage

The record title links to the subpage, and the Edit action goes to the same place. The subpage uses breadcrumbs, and its Save sits in the `Page` header like any other settings page. The table goes away while a record is open, so keep its search, filters and page somewhere that outlives it, and people find their results as they left them when they come back. Real screens usually keep the view in the URL or in user preferences; this example holds it above its routes.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.RecordsWithSubpages }
	source={ { code: RecordsSubpageSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

### Records that open a dialog

The dialog saves on its own. Cancel discards the draft, and Save applies it, closes the dialog and confirms with a snackbar. The same dialog adds new records.

The footer actions are the only way out: there is no close icon, and clicking outside does nothing, so people always choose between keeping and discarding their edits. Pressing Escape closes an untouched dialog, but asks first when there are unsaved edits.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.RecordsWithDialog }
	source={ { code: RecordsDialogSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>

### Records that open a drawer

The drawer works like the dialog, including closing only through its footer actions, with room for secondary actions. Revoking a key can't be undone, so it asks for confirmation in an `AlertDialog` with the `irreversible` intent, following [Destructive Actions](?path=/docs/design-system-patterns-destructive-actions--docs). Canceling returns focus to Revoke. After the key is revoked, focus moves to the next record, or to the previous one when it was last, and to Add API key when none remain.

<Canvas
	of={ SettingsPageStories.RecordsWithDrawer }
	source={ { code: RecordsDrawerSource, language: 'tsx', type: 'code' } }
/>
